title: Returns lag
brief: Write an operational analysis for the managers of three fictional branches of a tool library. In April, Harbor logged 510 loans, 48 overdue notices, 12 finally overdue items, and 7 days with a scanner outage. Hill logged 320, 19, 13, and 0. Park logged 400, 36, 16, and 3. In May, Harbor logged 540, 28, 14, and 1; Hill 300, 20, 11, and 0; Park 430, 22, 15, and 0. Notice totals count notifications; finally overdue items are unique and assessed after the manual reconciliation. Loans are transactions. At the beginning of May a reminder text was piloted only at Harbor. Managers want to know what changed, what they can attribute to reminders, and what records to collect next. Use the figures and give a recommendation.

02b0715b7a156273.text:
# Tool Library Operational Analysis: April–May Loans, Overdue Notices, and the Harbor Reminder Pilot

## Summary

Overdue notices fell sharply in May at Harbor and Park, while finally overdue items barely moved at any branch. The drop in notices tracks the end of the April scanner outages, not the reminder texts. Park had no reminders and saw almost the same decline as Harbor, and Harbor's count of finally overdue items rose from 12 to 14 during the pilot.

On these figures, no measurable reduction in overdue items can be attributed to reminders. The pilot has not been shown to fail; one month of branch totals, with an outage running through the baseline, cannot test it. The recommendation is to keep the pilot at Harbor in a form that can be tested, hold off on expanding it, and treat scanner reliability as the more pressing operational issue.

## The figures

Rates are per 100 loans. "Finally overdue" means unique items still overdue after manual reconciliation.

| Branch | Month | Loans | Notices | Notices per 100 loans | Finally overdue | Finally overdue per 100 loans | Outage days |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harbor | April | 510 | 48 | 9.4 | 12 | 2.4 | 7 |
| Harbor | May | 540 | 28 | 5.2 | 14 | 2.6 | 1 |
| Hill | April | 320 | 19 | 5.9 | 13 | 4.1 | 0 |
| Hill | May | 300 | 20 | 6.7 | 11 | 3.7 | 0 |
| Park | April | 400 | 36 | 9.0 | 16 | 4.0 | 3 |
| Park | May | 430 | 22 | 5.1 | 15 | 3.5 | 0 |
| All | April | 1,230 | 103 | 8.4 | 41 | 3.3 | 10 |
| All | May | 1,270 | 70 | 5.5 | 40 | 3.1 | 1 |

## What changed

**Loan volume shifted modestly.** Harbor rose by 30 loans (5.9%), Park rose by 30 (7.5%), and Hill fell by 20 (6.3%). Across the three branches, loans rose from 1,230 to 1,270, about 3%. None of these movements is large enough to explain the changes in notices.

**Notices fell by a third overall, and only at the branches that had outages.** Total notices dropped from 103 to 70.

- Harbor fell from 48 to 28, a drop of 20 notices (42%).
- Park fell from 36 to 22, a drop of 14 notices (39%).
- Hill was flat, moving from 19 to 20.

Per 100 loans, Harbor and Park moved almost in step: Harbor from 9.4 to 5.2, Park from 9.0 to 5.1. Hill drifted from 5.9 to 6.7, which reflects one more notice on 20 fewer loans.

**Finally overdue items were essentially unchanged.** The total went from 41 to 40. Harbor rose by two items (12 to 14), Hill fell by two (13 to 11), and Park fell by one (16 to 15). Counts this small move by one or two items from month to month for no reason at all, so none of these changes should be read as a trend.

**Scanner outages nearly disappeared.** April had 10 outage days (7 at Harbor, 3 at Park), and May had one, at Harbor.

**Harbor had the lowest rate of finally overdue items in both months.** Its rate was 2.4 per 100 loans in April, before any reminder was sent, against roughly 4 at Hill and Park. Harbor's better standing predates the pilot and cannot be credited to it.

## What explains the drop in notices

The pattern across branches points to the scanners. Three observations support this.

1. **The decline appears where outages ended, regardless of reminders.** Harbor (reminders, outage ended) and Park (no reminders, outage ended) both lost about 4 notices per 100 loans. Hill (no reminders, no outage in either month) did not decline.

2. **The ratio of notices to finally overdue items was inflated only during outages.** In the three outage-free branch-months, the system sent between 1.5 and 1.8 notices for every item that proved overdue (Hill 1.5 and 1.8; Park in May 1.5). In April, Park's ratio was 2.3 with three outage days and Harbor's was 4.0 with seven. In May, with one outage day, Harbor's ratio fell to 2.0.

3. **The outcome that survives reconciliation did not move.** If April's extra notices had reflected real lateness, more items should have been finally overdue in April than in May. They were not.

The likely mechanism is that returns made while a scanner was down were not recorded on time, so the system treated returned tools as still out and sent notices, which manual reconciliation later cleared. This is an inference from the totals, not something the data shows directly. It should be confirmed against the April reconciliation records at Harbor and Park.

If it holds, a large share of April's notices at those two branches were false alarms. Each one cost staff time in reconciliation and told a member who had returned a tool that they had not.

## What can be attributed to reminders

**On notices: very little, and possibly nothing.** The fair comparison for Harbor is Park, because both branches came out of an outage in May. Harbor's notice rate fell by 4.2 per 100 loans and Park's by 3.9. The difference of about 0.3 per 100 loans works out to roughly two notices on Harbor's May volume, which is well inside ordinary month-to-month variation.

A rougher check points the same way. Park shed 14 notices as three outage days disappeared, and Harbor shed 20 as six disappeared. Outage recovery alone could plausibly account for Harbor's whole decline.

Comparing Harbor with Hill would make reminders look effective, with a gap of about 5 notices per 100 loans. That comparison is misleading because Hill had no outage to recover from.

**On finally overdue items: nothing measurable.** Harbor's count rose from 12 to 14, and its rate from 2.4 to 2.6 per 100 loans, while the two branches without reminders fell slightly. This does not show that reminders made matters worse, since a two-item change is noise. It does mean there is no evidence in these figures that reminders reduced the number of tools that stay out late.

**Why the pilot is untested, not disproven.** Four limits prevent a firmer conclusion.

- **The baseline is contaminated.** Harbor's April notice count is distorted by seven outage days, so any April-to-May comparison at Harbor mixes the outage effect with the reminder effect.
- **The counts are small.** With 11 to 16 finally overdue items per branch per month, a reminder would need to cut overdue items by roughly half to stand out from chance in a single month.
- **Notices count notifications, not items.** One late tool may generate several notices, so a change in notices can reflect how long items stay late, how many are late, or how the system behaved.
- **The months may not line up.** A tool borrowed in late April and due in May appears in April's loans and May's overdue figures. Some of Harbor's May overdue items may come from loans made before the pilot began.

## What records to collect next

The current monthly totals cannot separate reminder effects from system effects. The following loan-level records would do so, and most should already exist in the lending system or the reconciliation log.

**For each loan:**
- Checkout date, due date, and actual return date and time.
- Whether the return was scanned or entered manually, and if manually, when it was entered.
- Whether a reminder text was sent, when, and whether it was delivered.
- Whether the member has a mobile number on file and has agreed to receive texts.
- Tool category and loan period, since long-loan or high-demand tools may behave differently.

**For each notice:**
- The item and loan it relates to, and the date sent, so that unique items notified can be counted alongside total notifications.
- The outcome: confirmed late, or cleared in reconciliation as already returned.

**For each finally overdue item:**
- Days late at the point of assessment and at eventual return.
- Whether the borrower had received a reminder.

**For each outage:**
- Start and end times (not only the count of affected days), which stations were affected, and how returns were handled during the outage.

**For reconciliation:**
- Staff time spent per month at each branch, which puts a cost on false notices.

With these records, three questions become answerable:

- How many April notices were false?
- What share of loans with a reminder came back on time, compared with loans without one?
- How much staff time does an outage day cost?

## Recommendation

**1. Do not credit the May decline in notices to reminders, and do not expand the pilot on the strength of it.** The decline is better explained by the scanners coming back, and the items-based measure did not improve at Harbor.

**2. Continue the pilot at Harbor for at least three more months, restructured so it can be tested.** Send reminders to half of Harbor's loans, split by a neutral rule such as odd and even membership numbers, instead of to all of them. The two groups will then share the same branch, month, staff, and scanner conditions, so any difference in late returns can be attributed to the text. At Harbor's volume, three months gives roughly 800 loans in each group. That is enough to detect a substantial effect, though not a slight one.

**3. Judge the pilot on items, not notifications.** The primary measure should be the share of loans returned after the due date, with finally overdue items per 100 loans as the secondary measure. Notice counts should be reported but not used as evidence of borrower behavior.

**4. Treat scanner reliability as the priority.** Ten outage days in April coincided with about 30 more notices than May's pattern would predict across Harbor and Park. Two steps would address this:

- Verify the false-notice explanation against April's reconciliation records.
- Adopt a standard outage procedure at all branches: record returns on paper with a timestamp, enter them the same day, and hold automated notices for items due during an outage until entry is complete.

**5. Start collecting the loan-level records at all three branches now.** This includes Hill and Park, even though they are not sending reminders. Their data provides the comparison if the pilot is later extended, and Hill's outage-free record is the cleanest baseline the library has.

**6. Review after the August figures are reconciled.** If loans with reminders show a clearly lower late-return rate than loans without, extend reminders to Park and Hill. If they do not, end the pilot and put the effort into outage handling, where the evidence of a problem is already clear.

# April–May operating review for Harbor, Hill, and Park

**Recommendation. Keep the reminder pilot at Harbor for a defined evaluation period and defer expansion to Hill and Park.** Harbor handled 30 more loans in May and logged 20 fewer overdue notices. That is a substantial change in notification activity, and it merits investigation. The reconciled count of overdue items, however, rose from 12 to 14. Harbor also went from seven days with a scanner outage to one. At Park, where managers did not pilot reminder texts, notices fell and scanner outages ended. The two months of branch totals establish what changed, but they cannot tell managers how much of the change the texts caused.

The immediate decision is what the pilot should accomplish. If the aim is to get tools back in time for the next borrower, the primary measure should be the share of items still overdue at a consistent point after their due date. If the aim also includes reducing staff work, managers should measure staff minutes spent on follow-up. A reminder could improve one outcome without improving the other. The decision about expansion should reflect the benefit the library actually sees and the cost of achieving it.

## What changed across the branches

The table gives April and May counts alongside rates per 100 loan transactions. Those rates put branches of different sizes on a common scale. A notice counts each notification, so multiple notices can concern the same item. The final overdue count includes each overdue item once after manual reconciliation. Because loans are transactions, neither rate gives the percentage of borrowers who were overdue.

| Branch | Loans, Apr → May | Notices, Apr → May | Notices per 100 loans | Final overdue items, Apr → May | Final overdue items per 100 loans | Scanner outage days, Apr → May |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Harbor | 510 → 540 | 48 → 28 | 9.41 → 5.19 | 12 → 14 | 2.35 → 2.59 | 7 → 1 |
| Hill | 320 → 300 | 19 → 20 | 5.94 → 6.67 | 13 → 11 | 4.06 → 3.67 | 0 → 0 |
| Park | 400 → 430 | 36 → 22 | 9.00 → 5.12 | 16 → 15 | 4.00 → 3.49 | 3 → 0 |
| **All branches** | **1,230 → 1,270** | **103 → 70** | **8.37 → 5.51** | **41 → 40** | **3.33 → 3.15** | **10 → 1** |

Across the library, loan volume grew by 40 transactions, or 3.3%, while notice volume fell by 33 notifications, or 32.0%. The final overdue count fell by just one item. Managers can report that the library handled more transactions with fewer logged notices and ended with nearly the same number of reconciled overdue items. Staff time savings remain unknown. An automated notice and a notice requiring a staff member to check a shelf and contact a borrower each add one to the total, although their demands on staff differ considerably.

**Harbor.** Notices fell by about 42%, from 48 to 28, even as loans grew by about 6%. The drop therefore survives adjustment for transaction volume. The notice rate fell by 4.23 per 100 loans, the largest decline of the three branches. Meanwhile, the final overdue count rose by two, and its rate edged up from 2.35 to 2.59 per 100 loans. Harbor still had the lowest final overdue rate of the three branches in both months. Its May figures give managers a reason to examine why fewer notices were logged, and little basis for concluding that the pilot improved or worsened returns.

**Hill.** With 20 fewer loans, Hill recorded one more notice and two fewer final overdue items. Its notice rate rose from 5.94 to 6.67 per 100 loans, while its final overdue rate fell from 4.06 to 3.67. Hill had uninterrupted scanner availability by the reported outage-day measure. It offers a view of ordinary month-to-month movement at a branch without the pilot or a change in reported outage days. Its experience also illustrates how notice activity and the eventual overdue count can move in opposite directions over the same period.

**Park.** Like Harbor, Park handled exactly 30 more loans in May. Its notices fell by 14, from 36 to 22, and its notice rate fell by 3.88 per 100 loans. Its May rate of 5.12 was almost identical to Harbor’s 5.19. Park’s final overdue count fell by one, and its three April scanner outage days fell to zero. Park gives managers the strongest reason for caution about attributing Harbor’s decline to texts. A branch without the pilot experienced nearly the same decline in notices per 100 loans while also recovering scanner availability.

## What managers can attribute to reminders

Harbor’s notice rate fell by only about 0.34 more notices per 100 loans than Park’s, using unrounded figures. Comparing Harbor with Hill gives a much larger apparent advantage because Hill’s notice rate rose. Neither comparison establishes how Harbor would have performed in May without reminders. April supplies only one pre-pilot observation, so managers cannot check whether Harbor normally tracks Park, Hill, or either branch closely. The variation between comparisons is itself important to the decision. A claim of pilot success would depend heavily on which branch managers chose as the benchmark.

Scanner availability offers a specific alternative explanation that staff can investigate. During an outage, a borrower might return a tool on time, but its return might reach the circulation system after an overdue notice has been generated. Reconciliation could then remove the item from the final overdue list while leaving the sent notice in the notification log. More reliable scanning in May could reduce these notices even if borrowers returned tools on exactly the same schedule. The outage totals are consistent with that account at Harbor and Park. They do not establish how many notices followed a delayed check-in, since the figures contain no outage times, affected transactions, or return timestamps.

The texts could also have made a difference that the final count misses. A borrower who responds to a reminder might return a tool before a second notice goes out. If that borrower would in any case have returned the tool before reconciliation, the text could reduce repeat notices and days overdue without changing the final count. There is also a basic counting question. If pilot texts were excluded from the 28 logged notices, Harbor may have shifted some contacts into a new channel. Until staff confirm the counting rule and tally the texts, managers cannot say whether borrowers received fewer messages overall.

Finally, dividing 14 final overdue items by 28 notices would not show that half of Harbor’s notices went unresolved. The two totals count different things and lack a link between a particular notice and its eventual outcome. Monthly loans are also an imperfect denominator for judging return performance. A loan opened late in May may come due in June, while a tool due in May may have gone out in April. The reported rates are suitable for comparing monthly operating volumes. Judging a reminder requires following the items that were eligible to receive it through their return deadlines.

## What to record next

Use a shared record format at all three branches. Start with circulation and notification data the library already captures, then add the few fields needed to distinguish borrower behavior from processing delays.

| Record | Fields and purpose |
|---|---|
| **Checkout and due date** | Link each checked-out item to its loan transaction, branch, and a privacy-preserving borrower identifier. Keep the original due date, any renewal date, and the revised due date so staff can reconstruct which items were due and eligible for a reminder. |
| **Reminder assignment and delivery** | Record eligibility, assignment to receive a text or usual service, scheduled send time, actual send time, and delivery status. Distinguish an assigned text that failed delivery from a loan that was never assigned a text. |
| **All borrower contacts** | Link each reminder and overdue notice to the relevant loan or items. Record the timestamp, channel, message type, and whether staff initiated it. Document which message types enter the monthly notice total so branches can compare like with like. |
| **Return and reconciliation** | Capture physical return time when known, system check-in time, and the item’s reconciled status at a common interval after the due date. Record corrections and their reasons. Preserve an unknown physical return time as unknown. |
| **Outages and staff effort** | Record outage start and end times, affected scanners or workflows, and when staff entered the backlog. Sample the minutes spent on manual check-ins, reconciliation, and borrower follow-up. Track text charges alongside labor. |

These records would let Harbor answer a practical question about an individual notice. Had the borrower already returned the tool when the notice went out? If so, the corrective action concerns return processing. If the tool was still out, staff can see whether the contact was the first or a repeat and how long the tool remained unavailable. Reviewing those cases at Park as well would help explain why the two branches recorded such similar notice declines.

## How to decide on expansion

For the next phase, randomly assign eligible Harbor borrowers to receive the pilot text or continue with usual service. Keep each borrower in the same group throughout the evaluation so frequent users have a consistent experience. Both groups should receive the usual overdue follow-up under the same rules. Comparing borrowers at the same branch over the same weeks gives both groups exposure to the same staffing calendar and scanner conditions. Analyze outcomes by original assignment, including failed deliveries, to estimate what Harbor can achieve with the service as operated.

Before enrollment, choose the follow-up interval, the smallest improvement that would justify the cost, and an enrollment target based on the number of eligible items due. Use the share of those items still overdue at the agreed interval as the primary return measure. Also report days overdue, repeat notices, total contacts across channels, and staff minutes. Follow the last enrolled items through the full interval before comparing groups. With only 12 and 14 final overdue items in Harbor’s two monthly reports, another small swing in counts could easily leave managers uncertain. Report the estimated difference alongside its uncertainty.

Expand if the evaluation shows a worthwhile improvement in returns or a documented operating saving at an acceptable cost, with borrower contact volume taken into account. If most avoidable notices concern tools already returned, prioritize recording returns promptly during outages. If reminders shorten the time tools spend overdue, quantify those recovered days of availability when deciding whether to expand. That gives all three managers a decision grounded in what matters at the lending desk and on the shelf.

f0e0589e1aeb29f1.text:
# Tool library operations review: April and May

Harbor sent 20 fewer overdue notices in May while recording 30 more loans. Its count of unique items still overdue after manual reconciliation rose from 12 to 14. Park, which did not pilot reminder texts, also recorded more loans and substantially fewer notices, while its final overdue count fell by one. Across all three branches, notices fell from 103 to 70, and the final overdue count fell from 41 to 40.

The May figures establish that Harbor sent fewer notices during the first month of the reminder pilot. They do not establish that the texts caused the decline or improved returns. Harbor’s scanner outages also fell from seven days to one, and Park saw a similar drop in notices as its outages fell from three days to zero. Keep the pilot at Harbor and collect loan-level records for a controlled follow-up. The decision to expand should rest on whether texts improve returns, with changes in notice workload measured separately.

## What changed

Each cell shows the April figure followed by the May figure.

| Branch | Loan transactions | Overdue notices | Unique items still overdue after reconciliation | Scanner outage days |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Harbor | 510 → 540 | 48 → 28 | 12 → 14 | 7 → 1 |
| Hill | 320 → 300 | 19 → 20 | 13 → 11 | 0 → 0 |
| Park | 400 → 430 | 36 → 22 | 16 → 15 | 3 → 0 |
| **Total** | **1,230 → 1,270** | **103 → 70** | **41 → 40** | **10 → 1** |

**Harbor** handled about 6% more loan transactions and sent about 42% fewer overdue notices. Notices per 100 recorded loans fell from 9.4 to 5.2. Meanwhile, the final overdue count increased by two, from 2.4 to 2.6 items per 100 loans. The branch therefore saw a substantial reduction in outgoing overdue notices while ending the reconciliation process with slightly more overdue items. The lower notice volume may have reduced some follow-up work, but the figures contain no measure of staff time or total communications, including the new texts.

**Hill** handled 20 fewer loan transactions and sent one more notice. Notices per 100 loans rose from 5.9 to 6.7. The final overdue count fell by two, from 4.1 to 3.7 items per 100 loans. Hill had no scanner outages in either month. Its results show that the two overdue measures can move in different directions even with no recorded scanner interruption. With changes of only one or two in the raw counts, Hill’s two months provide little evidence of a sustained change.

**Park** handled 30 more loan transactions and sent 14 fewer notices, a decline of about 39%. Notices per 100 loans fell from 9.0 to 5.1, close to Harbor’s May level and close to Harbor’s decline of 4.2 notices per 100 loans. Park’s final overdue count fell from 16 to 15, or from 4.0 to 3.5 items per 100 loans. Park reached a similar notice result without piloting texts. Its scanner was also available on more days in May.

Across the three branches, 40 additional loan transactions coincided with 33 fewer notices. Harbor and Park together sent 34 fewer notices, and Hill sent one more. The systemwide notice count fell by about 32%, from 8.4 to 5.5 notices per 100 loans, while the final overdue count changed by one item. The largest measured change was in how many notices went out. The count that remained after reconciliation was broadly stable.

## What the figures say about reminders

Notice totals count notifications, so several notices may concern the same item. A branch could send fewer notices because fewer items reached the first overdue threshold, because it sent fewer repeat notices, or because it changed when notices went out. Those possibilities have different implications for returns and staff workload. The monthly totals cannot distinguish among them.

The rates per 100 loans help account for differences in recorded transaction volume, but they are descriptive ratios. The notices or reconciled items counted in May may relate to loans made in April, and some loans made in late May may come due in June. The number of unique items remaining overdue after reconciliation also does not capture every item returned late. An item could have triggered a notice and then been returned before the final count. To judge whether more borrowers returned tools on time, managers need to follow loans by due date and link each loan to its return and notification history.

Harbor’s decline is consistent with several effects a text reminder could have. If texts prompted borrowers to return tools before the first overdue notice, both first notices and late returns could have fallen. If the text took the place of a communication previously counted as an overdue notice, the notice count could have fallen even if return behavior stayed the same. The reported totals give no indication of how many borrowers were eligible, how many texts were delivered, or whether the texts went out before the due date or after it. Harbor’s increase of two in the final overdue count likewise cannot establish that reminders made returns worse. The count is small, and the set of items due may have differed between months.

Comparing branches helps put the pilot in context. Harbor’s notice rate fell about 4.2 per 100 loans, and Park’s fell about 3.9 without texts. Hill moved in the opposite direction. Combining Hill and Park produces a smaller decline of about 1.9 notices per 100 loans, but subtracting that decline from Harbor’s would give a misleading estimate of the reminder effect. The comparison branches had different changes in volume and scanner availability, and there is only one month before the pilot to show how their numbers usually move relative to Harbor’s.

Scanner availability is a plausible contributor that can be investigated with records. For example, if staff accepted returns during an outage but logged them later, notices could have gone out for tools already back at the branch. Manual reconciliation could then remove those tools from the final overdue count. That sequence would produce more notices without an equivalent increase in finally overdue items. The outage day totals do not show whether it happened, how long each interruption lasted, or how many returns were affected. The same uncertainty applies to any changes in notice scheduling or reconciliation practice.

## Records to collect next

Use a stable loan identifier to link the following records. Start by recovering the April and May history where available, and use the same definitions and observation windows across branches going forward.

1. **Loan and return history.** Record the branch, loan ID, item ID, checkout time, original and revised due dates, renewals, physical return time where known, and system check-in time. Retain a borrower identifier suitable for linking multiple loans without putting names or phone numbers into the analysis file. Group loans by the date they were due and allow each group the same follow-up period. This makes it possible to calculate the share returned by the due date, the share still out after a defined interval, and the number of unique items still overdue after reconciliation.

2. **Reminder and notice activity.** Record who was eligible for the pilot, whether a reminder was assigned, its scheduled and actual send times, and its delivery status. For each overdue notice, record its time, channel, and whether it was the first or a repeat for that loan. Include any rule that suppresses or replaces a notice after a text. These records will show whether fewer loans generated notices, each affected loan generated fewer notices, or the branch shifted traffic from one channel to another.

3. **Scanner interruptions and manual reconciliation.** Record outage start and end times, which operations were affected, and when any backlog was entered. Where staff accept a return manually, capture when they received the tool and when they updated the loan record. Log any notice sent in between, along with the reconciliation date and the reason for correcting the overdue status. This will show how often delayed check-ins lead to notices and whether that pattern differs across branches or months.

4. **Changes in operating practices and staff effort.** Record effective dates for changes in due dates, grace periods, notice schedules, opening hours, and reconciliation procedures. If reducing staff work is an objective, track time spent handling notices, resolving disputed overdue records, and reconciling returns. Automated notices and manual follow-up can have very different costs, so the notification count alone cannot answer whether the pilot saved time.

## Recommendation

Continue the Harbor pilot as a controlled trial before expanding it. Randomly assign eligible Harbor borrowers to receive the pilot text or continue with the standard process, keeping the usual overdue notice and reconciliation rules consistent across groups. Assign at the borrower level so that someone with multiple loans receives a consistent experience. Compare outcomes according to the original assignment and track delivery failures separately. Running both groups at Harbor over the same weeks gives them the same branch operating conditions, including scanner interruptions, and makes the effect of offering the text easier to estimate.

Use the share of loans returned by their due date as the primary measure. Track the share still out after a fixed follow-up interval and the reconciled count of unique overdue items to see whether any improvement persists. Review first notices, repeat notices, total communications, and staff time as operational measures. Agree before the trial on an improvement large enough to justify expansion, and collect enough completed due-date groups to assess it. With only 12 to 16 finally overdue items per branch per month in the current figures, one month’s movement in that count is a weak basis for a rollout decision.

In parallel, examine any April and May return logs that can link scanner downtime to delayed check-ins and notices. Confirmed cases can guide changes to how branches record manual returns and process notices during a backlog. If the Harbor trial shows a meaningful improvement in returns, use that result to decide whether to extend the texts. If it shows fewer overdue notices with similar return outcomes, judge the text on measured staff time and total contact volume and treat any expansion as a change to the communications process.
